rules.text_en: A message is sent as a single unit; do not add chunk headers or separators (e.g., `[part X/Y]`, `---END---`). A line starting with `^` is a directive: an instruction from sender to receiver. The decoder must preserve the `^` and the rest of the line verbatim; the receiver treats the line as actionable. Any other line is narrative content, preserved verbatim, and is not an instruction. When the message consists primarily of instructions or actionable items, write each as a directive line; use plain text lines only for explanatory context that cannot be framed as an instruction.

The sender may write any line in minimal form: omit punctuation (.,:;!?-) and capitalization except where required for numeric literals, unit symbols, or alphanumeric identifiers. The decoder must reconstruct the intended meaning, inferring appropriate punctuation and capitalization as needed. In plain text lines, the sender must omit the following where meaning remains clear: articles 'a', 'an', 'the'; prepositions 'of', 'in', 'for', 'on', 'at', 'to'; copula verbs 'is', 'are', 'was', 'were', 'be', 'been'; auxiliary verbs 'has', 'have', 'had' before past participles; relative pronouns 'that', 'which', 'who', 'whom' introducing a subordinate clause. Do not omit binding words (and, with, because, or, but, so) that link clauses or items. The decoder must infer omitted words.

In numeric literals, preserve all punctuation that affects value. The decimal point must be preserved exactly. A leading zero before a decimal point may be omitted only if the value is less than 1; the decoder must interpret '.8' as '0.8'. In any numeric literal immediately followed by a unit symbol or constituting a percentage, the decimal point must be preserved. In numeric ranges, preserve the delimiter (hyphen, en-dash, colon) exactly; do not replace it with a space. The decoder must interpret the delimiter as indicating a continuous range between the two values. Preserve monetary amounts exactly as in the original, including the currency symbol, decimal point, and any commas as thousand separators; do not omit the currency symbol or decimal point under minimal-form allowances. The decoder must treat the monetary amount as a single numeric entity with its intended value and unit.

Alphanumeric identifiers include command-line flags, API endpoints, zone names, file paths, email addresses, and any technical syntax where hyphens, underscores, slashes, and equals are part of the identifier. The sender must preserve all punctuation and capitalization within such identifiers exactly as in the original; the minimal-form allowance to omit punctuation does not apply within these identifiers. Hyphenated alphanumeric identifiers must preserve the hyphen and capitalization of each segment exactly. An opaque identifier is any string that serves as a unique reference (serial number, order ID, hash, UUID, code) where its exact characters are meaningful. The sender must preserve opaque identifiers exactly as in the original, including all internal punctuation, digits, case, and whitespace. If the identifier contains punctuation or whitespace that could cause tokenizer splitting, enclose it in backticks and join segments with underscores inside the backticks. If the identifier contains no punctuation or whitespace and tokenizes as a single token, transmit it verbatim without backticks unless it repeats at least 3 times, in which case an alias is mandatory. The decoder must remove backticks when present, reconstruct the original identifier verbatim, and validate character-for-character match with the source; any mismatch renders the message non-compliant. When a colon is part of a technical identifier, tag, or environment specifier, preserve the colon and the adjacent word as a single unbroken unit; do not treat the colon as a directive slot separator. The decoder must interpret the colon as binding the qualifier to its preceding noun phrase.

The sender must preserve all named entities (people, organizations, dates, deadlines, penalty clauses), key quantities, and explicit stakes from the original message. Omitting these constitutes a violation of the language's purpose, even if the literal encoding is rule-compliant. In any line, preserve all location names, system identifiers, region tags, and environment specifiers exactly as in the original, including capitalization and punctuation; do not omit them under any compression allowance. Within any line, preserve all explicit times, deadlines, and numeric qualifiers exactly, including colons and leading zeros if present; do not omit them under minimal form. In plain text lines, preserve ordinal words and sequence indicators exactly as in the original; do not omit them under minimal-form allowances. The decoder must interpret these words as specifying exact order or position. In plain text lines preceding a directive, preserve all comparative qualifiers and logical connectors that explain the rationale for that directive; do not omit them under minimal-form allowances. The decoder must interpret these qualifiers as explaining why the directive applies. In plain text lines that contain a conditional or sequential chain, preserve the exact sequence words 'if', 'then', 'unless', 'because', and 'so' exactly as in the original; do not omit them under minimal-form allowances. The decoder must interpret these preserved words as marking the intended logical relationship between clauses. When the source message uses a colloquial abbreviation of a technical unit, preserve that abbreviation as written. The decoder must interpret the abbreviation as the same unit intended by the source, not expand it to a formal unit unless the expansion is explicitly present in the source.

Within a message, the sender may define an abbreviation for any string that repeats at least 3 times by writing `@short=long_form` on its own line. Thereafter, `@short` may be used in place of the full form. The decoder must substitute the original exactly. The sender must ensure token savings: definition tokens + (uses × abbreviation tokens) < uses × original tokens. For opaque identifiers, the long_form uses the identifier's encoded form. For curly-brace or angle-bracket bundles, include the full bundle. For action verbs in directive lines, the abbreviation may be used in any directive line. For common nouns in plain text lines, join words with underscores.

For directive lines, the sender may use positional slots to imply function words. Recommended order: action, object, condition, deadline, rationale. Omit prepositions and articles where the slot order conveys the relationship. The decoder must infer the intended meaning. When a directive line contains a list of items sharing the same action and qualifier, the sender may write the action and qualifier once, followed by a colon and then the list of items separated by commas. The decoder must interpret each list item as receiving the same action and qualifier. If any item has a distinct qualifier, it must be written as a separate directive. In directive lines, the sender may replace the prepositions 'by', 'at', 'to', 'for' when followed by a time, deadline, or recipient with a colon. The colon attaches the following phrase to the preceding slot. The decoder must interpret the colon as the appropriate preposition. In directive lines, the sender may replace 'and' or 'or' connecting multiple arguments with `+` or `|`. The decoder must interpret `+` as 'and' and `|` as 'or'. If an action requires a preposition, preserve it or use a colon. In directive lines, the sender may replace 'greater than', 'older than', 'less than', 'newer than' with `>` or `<`. The decoder must interpret `>` as 'older than' when followed by a duration and as 'greater than' when followed by a plain numeric value; `<` means 'newer than' for durations and 'less than' for plain numeric values.

The sender must preserve all core contextual facts from the original message: event names, venues, key constraints, deadlines, attendee counts, capacity limits, and explicit stakes. These must appear as plain text lines before the directives they justify. Omitting such context renders the message non-compliant.

Revise rule-442's opaque identifier clause to mandate backticks for all opaque identifiers, eliminating the exception for identifiers with no punctuation or whitespace. Replace the current clause beginning 'If the identifier contains no punctuation or whitespace and tokenizes as a single token, transmit it verbatim without backticks unless it repeats at least 3 times, in which case an alias is mandatory' with: 'The sender must enclose every opaque identifier in backticks to form a single atomic token; inside the backticks, join any segments separated by punctuation or whitespace with underscores to ensure tokenizer integrity. The decoder must remove the backticks and reconstruct the original identifier verbatim, validating character-for-character match with the source; any mismatch renders the message non-compliant. If an opaque identifier repeats at least 3 times, an alias under rule-444 is mandatory.' This ensures atomic preservation for all opaque identifiers, directly satisfying the fault invariant.

Revise rule-449 to forbid underscore substitution inside backticks for opaque identifiers. Replace the clause 'inside the backticks, join any segments separated by punctuation or whitespace with underscores to ensure tokenizer integrity' with: 'inside the backticks, preserve every character, punctuation, digit, case, and whitespace exactly as in the source, without substituting any punctuation or spaces with underscores or altering any character. The encoder must rely on the backticks alone to form a single atomic token; if tokenizer splitting occurs, the message is non-compliant and the encoder must define an alias per rule-444.' The decoder requirement remains: remove backticks and validate character-for-character match. This ensures exact preservation without internal modifications that could corrupt the identifier's exact form, directly satisfying the opaque identifier fault invariant.

In any line describing a measured fact—including allocations, conditions, thresholds, or comparisons—the sender must treat the entire measured fact as a single atomic token by surrounding it with angle brackets: <numeric value unit comparison phrase or symbol relational preposition target identifier>. The decoder must remove the angle brackets and reconstruct the original spacing and punctuation verbatim, preserving numeric precision, units, thresholds, and comparison direction exactly as in the source. The decoder must validate that the reconstructed bundle matches the source character-for-character; any mismatch renders the message non-compliant. This rule applies to all measured facts not already covered by a more specific atomic encoding (e.g., opaque identifiers per rule-452). Example: 'alert if temperature <5°C' encodes as 'alert if <temperature <5°C>' and decodes as 'alert if temperature <5°C'; 'allocate 10 GB to node-7' encodes as 'allocate <10 GB to node-7>' and decodes as 'allocate 10 GB to node-7'.

In any line describing a measured fact—including allocations, conditions, thresholds, or comparisons—the sender must treat the entire measured fact as a single atomic token by surrounding it with angle brackets: <numeric value unit comparison phrase or symbol relational preposition target identifier>. The decoder must remove the angle brackets and reconstruct the original spacing and punctuation verbatim, preserving numeric precision, units, thresholds, and comparison direction exactly as in the source. The decoder must validate both: (1) character‑for‑character match between the reconstructed bundle and the source; (2) that the reconstructed bundle contains every original component—value, unit, comparison phrase or symbol, relational preposition (if any), and target identifier (if any)—without omission, alteration, or splitting. If either validation fails, the message is non‑compliant. This rule applies to all measured facts not already covered by a more specific atomic encoding (e.g., opaque identifiers per rule‑452). Example: 'alert if temperature <5°C' encodes as 'alert if <temperature <5°C>' and decodes as 'alert if temperature <5°C'; 'allocate 10 GB to node‑7' encodes as 'allocate <10 GB to node‑7>' and decodes as 'allocate 10 GB to node‑7'.

In any line describing a temporal constraint—including absolute times (e.g., '04:30 PM EST'), relative deadlines (e.g., 'by tomorrow'), date ranges (e.g., '2025‑03‑15 to 2025‑03‑17'), durations (e.g., 'for 30 days'), and ordering relationships (e.g., 'before event start', 'after step 3')—the sender must treat the entire temporal phrase as a single atomic token by surrounding it with angle brackets: <temporal phrase>. The decoder must remove the angle brackets and reconstruct the original wording, spacing, punctuation, and relational ordering exactly as in the source, without normalizing, abbreviating, omitting, or altering any component. The decoder must validate that the reconstructed phrase matches the source character‑for‑character; if any component differs, the message is non‑compliant. This rule applies to all temporal constraints not already covered by a more specific atomic encoding (e.g., opaque identifiers per rule‑452). Example: 'submit report <by 04:30 PM EST>' decodes as 'submit report by 04:30 PM EST'; 'maintenance window <from 2025‑03‑15 to 2025‑03‑17>' decodes as 'maintenance window from 2025‑03‑15 to 2025‑03‑17'.

Revise rule‑455 to explicitly forbid decoder normalization and require verbatim literal output. Replace the sentence 'The decoder must remove the angle brackets and reconstruct the original wording, spacing, punctuation, and relational ordering exactly as in the source, without normalizing, abbreviating, omitting, or altering any component.' with: 'The decoder must treat the content inside the angle brackets as a literal string; it must remove the angle brackets and output that string verbatim, without parsing, normalizing, abbreviating, reordering, omitting, or altering any character. The decoder must then validate that the verbatim output matches the source character‑for‑character; if any component differs, the message is non‑compliant.' This ensures the temporal phrase is preserved exactly as written, satisfying the fault invariant.

In any line containing a temporal expression—including times, deadlines, ranges, durations, and ordering relationships—the sender must identify the complete contiguous sequence of words that constitute the temporal expression. The sequence begins with the first relational preposition (e.g., 'by', 'at', 'from', 'to', 'before', 'after', 'until', 'for') or subordinating conjunction (e.g., 'when', 'once', 'as soon as') that links the temporal element to the surrounding context and includes every subsequent word up to and including the last temporal element (time, date, range, duration, or event reference). The sender must treat this entire sequence as a single atomic token by surrounding it with angle brackets: <complete temporal phrase>. The encoder must verify that the enclosed phrase contains every original component—times, dates, ranges, durations, ordering words, and all linking prepositions/conjunctions—without omission, normalization, abbreviation, or alteration. The decoder must remove the angle brackets and output the enclosed string verbatim, without parsing, normalizing, abbreviating, reordering, omitting, or altering any character. The decoder must validate that the verbatim output matches the source character‑for‑character; if any component differs, the message is non‑compliant. This rule applies to all temporal constraints not already covered by a more specific atomic encoding (e.g., opaque identifiers per rule‑452). Example: 'submit report by 04:30 PM EST' encodes as 'submit report <by 04:30 PM EST>'; 'maintenance window from 2025‑03‑15 to 2025‑03‑17' encodes as 'maintenance window <from 2025‑03‑15 to 2025‑03‑17>'; 'wait until the start of event' encodes as 'wait <until the start of event>'.
